clauses.en: The nondual method is to set up a distinction and to state with it the relations it rests on, what it applies to and what it leaves out.
The nondual method is a requirement of method, not a proof.
A representation states the view used, together with what its representing fixes.
Not is: if it holds, there is a contradiction;
Not yet is: what is read up to this point excludes neither its holding nor its not holding.
Necessarily is: it holds on every branch that opens;
Possibly is: it holds on some branch that opens, and which branch it is is shown.
Decided is: holds or does not hold.
For every claim, there is a number that is one where the claim holds and zero where it does not hold, exactly where the claim is decided (for the count of a family, see 三·七).
Cannot be refuted is: its denial cannot stand.
For every claim, that it is decided cannot be refuted.
Double-negation stability is, for a claim: if it cannot be refuted, it holds.
A decided claim has double-negation stability;
Equality of natural numbers has double-negation stability.
All is: it holds of every member under consideration;
None is: it holds of no member under consideration;
None not is: there is no member under consideration of which it does not hold.
For every family, if for each member that it holds cannot be refuted, then that it holds of all cannot be refuted.
Recurs is: something holds at arbitrarily late steps; after every step there is a step at which it holds.
A derivation is a finite tree that infers a claim from a basis and from if-clauses.
For every derivation, the claim it infers holds at every configuration at which the basis and the if-clauses all hold.
An if-clause places a hypothesis in a claim: the claim holds where the hypothesis holds.
For every derivation, if the basis holds throughout a region, then a claim inferred under if-clauses holds at every configuration in the region at which its if-clauses hold;
if the if-clauses also hold throughout the region, then the inferred claim holds throughout the region.
Then is: where the former holds, the latter holds, without stating that the former holds;
Therefore is: the former holds, and the latter is inferred from it.
There is a derivation whose configurations take two values and whose basis holds everywhere: a claim is inferred with itself as its if-clause;
discharging that if-clause, the resulting claim with then is inferred without if-clauses;
and the claim itself cannot be inferred without if-clauses.
A counterexample is a configuration in a region at which a claim does not hold.
For every derivation, if the basis holds throughout a region, then for a claim inferred without if-clauses there is no configuration in the region at which it does not hold;
if the basis holds throughout a region and there is a configuration in the region at which a claim does not hold, then that claim cannot be inferred without if-clauses.

title_en: What is inferred and the basis

clauses.en: For every derivation, every claim it infers without if-clauses holds throughout a region exactly where its basis holds throughout the region.
If the basis holds throughout a region, then, when a claim inferred without if-clauses is added to the basis, every claim the new basis infers without if-clauses still holds throughout the region.
A sufficient condition is: where this is, that holds.
A proof is a claim that has been checked, together with its check.
Every proof of the core depends on no axiom (no propext, Quot.sound, Classical.choice).
A supposition is what is stated and not asserted;
in a proof it is a definition or an if-clause, not an axiom.
The ethical suppositions are two: the first fixes the scope of significance and orders nothing; the second alone fixes which of several courses is better;
every statement of which course is better (the ethical order) cites the second alone.
Any other order, such as the trade-offs a practical commitment fixes, or the order a single one uses of its own, names its own supposition and is not the ethical order.
A theorem without premise holds in every world so represented; the local hypotheses it uses are written as if-clauses, and no supposition is taken as an if-clause.
A theorem under stated premises holds wherever the suppositions it names hold.
A reading (AI, D62) is an interpretation taken of the content of what is proved or of the structure of an ancient text, taken together with its argument;
a reading entered in the record of decisions is marked with its decision number.
A reading does not change a proof; a better argument changes the reading.
Left open is what is not a proof, not a supposition and not a reading, and writes out what is missing.
Weakly decided is: does not hold, or cannot be refuted.
A decided claim is weakly decided.
That every claim is weakly decided is a supposition.
Excluded middle is: every claim holds or does not hold; it is a supposition.
The limited principle of omniscience is: for every sequence of holding or not holding along the steps, either it holds at some step or it does not hold at any step; it is a supposition.

The weak limited principle of omniscience is: for every sequence of holding or not holding along the steps, either it does not hold at any step, or it is not the case that it does not hold at any step; it is a supposition.
If the limited principle of omniscience holds, then the weak limited principle of omniscience holds.
Markov's principle is: for every sequence of holding or not holding along the steps, if it is not the case that it does not hold at any step, then it holds at some step; it is a supposition.
Agreement is: for the structure a passage of an ancient text states, the spine has a proved theorem with the same relations, hypotheses and direction.
Scope restriction is: the spine gives the exact range within which what a passage of an ancient text states holds, and changes its universal form.
Divergence is: the theory does not assert what the ancient text asserts, or what the text asserts conflicts with the structure of the theory.

The unfolding is one unfolding of relations: it is represented by a type of relata, which at each step have levels, activity, conditions, needs and draws, and between steps take from and give to one another (for condition, level, activity, dependence, need and draws see 一·二; for uptake and replenishment see 一·十一).
A relatum is a term of the relations of this unfolding.
The whole of the unfolding is everything of the unfolding;
a part is a share of the whole of the unfolding.
Formation is the role of a relatum that depends on others and draws from them;
condition is the role of a relatum that others depend on: one relatum can hold both roles.
A level is the amount of a condition at a step;
activity is a formation being in operation at a step.
Dependence is the relation by which a formation at a step depends on a condition;
need is its threshold amount, the number the level of the condition must reach.
Draws is the relation by which a formation at a step uses a condition; only whether it draws or not is recorded, not the amount.
A web is what records, at each step, the levels of the conditions, the activity of the formations, and their conditions, needs and draws;
what it records can change from step to step.
A configuration is what the unfolding is at a step.
A move is what passes between steps.
A step is the natural-number order by which all relata are counted in common.
A claim is what can be said to hold or not hold at a configuration; it need not be decided.
A model is what gives one value to each item it applies to;
a reading is giving values to configurations through a model;
reading off an amount from what makes it up is also called a reading.
A process is the admissible transitions between configurations: a configuration goes by a move to a configuration.

A run is an infinite actual execution of a process: at each step there is a configuration and a move, and every passage from this configuration by this move to the next configuration is admissible in its process.

title_en: Comes to be and ceases to be

clauses.en: Comes to be is: a claim does not hold at a step and holds at the next step;
ceases to be is: a claim holds at a step and does not hold at the next step.
For every claim decided at each step, if it holds at some step and from then on never ceases to be, then from then on it holds at every step;
for every claim, if it does not hold at some step and from then on never comes to be, then from then on it holds at no step, without requiring that it be decided.
Becoming is the common name of the forming, keeping, transformation and dissolving of relations (for forms and dissolves see 二·二, for kept see 二·三, for transformation see 三·十三;
for reading see 一·三);
generation and degeneration are both within it (六·六).

For every claim, its coming to be and ceasing to be across a step, read on activity, read on dependence and read on standing as a condition, are one becoming with three readings, and this holds by definition.
A law is a process in which a configuration and a move have at most one configuration as outcome.
The law shown is the process a history shows, which admits only the transitions the history passes through.
Every history is a run of its law shown;
every process has a history as a run exactly where it contains every transition of the law shown of that history: the law shown is the least process that has this history as a run.

title_en: When the law shown is a law

clauses.en: A consistent history is one in which, whenever it is twice at the same configuration with the same move, the outcomes are the same.
The law shown of a history is a law exactly where the history is consistent;
there is a law that has this history as a run, also exactly where this holds.
Every law that has a history as a run gives, at every transition the history shows, the same outcome as the law shown.

title_en: Histories fix the law up to dead ends

clauses.en: A region of histories is the whole of the runs of some process exactly where every run of the process it shows lies in it.
Two processes have the same runs exactly where they have the same transitions that some run passes through;
a transition of a process that no run passes through is shown by no history.
Reading the move into the configuration and taking it out again leaves the configurations and moves of a run as they were.
After the move is read in, a transition to a configuration admits any move after it;
the process with the move read in is a law exactly where the original process is a law and, where there is any transition, there is only one kind of move.

title_en: Flow, uptake, replenishment, taking and giving

clauses.en: Flow is the amounts relata take from and give to one another across a step: at each step each relatum taking part has, at each condition, an amount it takes and an amount it gives.
Uptake is the amount relata taking part take from a condition;
replenishment is the amount relata taking part give to a condition.
Taking and giving is the flow of one step read as one move.
A world is a type of relata whose configuration at each step is a configuration of a web and whose move between steps is a taking and giving: a run of the process that admits every transition.
Every world is a run of its law shown, and this run read as a world is that world;
for every run whose configurations are configurations of a web and whose moves are takings and givings, read as a world, its configuration of the web at each step is its configuration.
Formation and condition (一·二) are two roles of one relatum.
Every web that divides formations and conditions into two types can be read as a web of one type of relata, and so read it makes a world.
The space of worlds is the type of every world represented.
A theorem without supposition holds in every world of the space of worlds.
A supposition of a world is a requirement that marks off a part of the space of worlds: some worlds fit it and some do not.
Balance is: the level of a condition after the step plus its joint taking equals its level before the step plus what is given to it in all.
Under balance, for every family, the total level after the step plus what is taken from it equals the total level before the step plus what is given to it;
across a stretch of steps, the two are also equal.
Under balance, a level that rises across a step has something given to it, and a level that falls across a step has something taken from it.
A world balances exactly where its levels move at each step, with its taking and giving as the move, by the process of balance;
and also exactly where every transition of its law shown is a transition of the process of balance.
Takers are those taking part that take something from the family across a step;
renewers are those taking part that give something to the family across a step.
More without end is: for every number, from some step on the number of takers at every step is not less than that number.
Only the active give: every renewer is active at its step;
only the active take, and they take only from what they draw on: every taker is active at its step and draws on what it takes from: both are suppositions of a world (一·十四).

The rest of the whole is what of the whole of the unfolding the world does not contain, counted as one relatum, whose taking and giving is read off from the difference between the change of levels and the taking and giving within the world.

Counting the rest of the whole, and reading activity as taking part with some taking or giving and draws as taking something, every world balances, only the active give, only the active take, and they take only from what they draw on.
A world balances by itself exactly where, with the rest of the whole counted, the rest is inactive at every step;
the becoming of a world read by levels and read by taking and giving: the two readings show the same at every step exactly where the world balances;
counting the rest of the whole, the two readings are the same in every world at every step.

title_en: Moves of the part and moves of the rest

clauses.en: Take a part and the rest of the whole as two components of one configuration, the two moving together at each step by one move.
A move fixed only by the configuration of the part (the same configuration of the part, the same move), whatever the configuration of the rest, is a move of the part;
one fixed only by the configuration of the rest is a move of the rest;
a move is both exactly where it is the same everywhere: so every move that differs at two places is fixed alone by at most one side.
There is a move that comes from the relation between the part and the rest, which neither fixes alone.

If the process of the part is a law and the move is a move of the part, then the part has its own law: for two runs of the whole of the unfolding in which the part starts at the same configuration, however the rest starts and runs, the part is the same at every step.

If the next configuration of the rest is fixed by a model (一·三) of its configuration and the move, and the move is a move of the part, then the run of the rest is the run, from its starting configuration, under the moves that the configurations of the part fix step by step: what the part does, the rest receives.
A frame is a process in which each configuration is attached to the claims that hold at it (for claim see 一·三).
Along a run, a frame is a world: its relata are the claims, a claim holding is its relatum being active, and a claim coming to be is the activity of its relatum coming to be.
With the configurations as the claims, if the worlds of two runs have the same activity everywhere, then the two runs have the same configuration at every step.
View is the common name of process, frame and world.
For every law given by a model that assigns each configuration its next configuration, the orbit from a configuration is a run of its process;
every run of its process is the orbit from its starting configuration.
A name is that by which what is read is referred to: the value a reading gives to what it reads.
A course is the values of the configurations of a history through a model, step by step.

Every sequence of values along the steps is a course: taking the passage from each step to its next as the law and these values as the model, two steps are alike exactly where the values from the two steps on are the same step by step;
if two steps are alike, their next steps are alike too: the configurations of a course and its law are both read off the course, and no configurations need be given.
For a run of a law, its course through a model is the same from two steps on exactly where, with the law shown through this model, the configurations at the two steps are alike.
Two configurations whose courses under a law through a model are the same at every step are said to have the same course.

Alike is: two configurations are linked by a relation such that, for any two configurations it links, the same claims hold at both, and whenever one makes a transition, the other makes a transition by the same move to one it links.
Two configurations under a law shown through a model are alike exactly where they have the same course.
A frame is determined up to likeness at a configuration where any two outcomes of one move from this configuration are alike;
being determined up to likeness carries over along likeness.
If the claims are the names of the configurations, then the process is a law exactly where the frame is determined up to likeness at every configuration.

title_en: A configuration is how it relates

clauses.en: For alike configurations, after the same sequence of moves the claims that can hold are the same.
A description that makes sense is a reading that puts together only configurations that are alike and puts together all that are alike;
if a frame is determined up to likeness at every configuration, then a description that makes sense carries a law.

If two frames are each determined up to likeness at every configuration, then two configurations are alike exactly where the sequences of moves admissible from them are the same and, after the same sequence of moves, the claims that can hold are the same.

For every whole of the unfolding divided into two parts, recording what each allows and describing them apart adds nothing absent exactly where whatever one part allows combines with whatever the other part allows;
otherwise what is left out is exactly their relation, which shows up again as extra combinations.
There are three parts such that what any two of them allow combines freely, while what the three allow does not.
Gluing is: what the contexts show at a configuration fits one context-free value: for every context that holds a claim, what it shows is this value at the claim.
If every claim is held by some context, the contexts glue at a configuration exactly where every two contexts that both hold a claim show the same there.
Contextual composition is: readings each hold in their context, and together they make one world.
Along a run, claims indexed by context are all relata of one world, active exactly where their context holds them and shows this value, without requiring gluing.
If every claim is held by some context, then there is a context-free frame that fits the contexts exactly where they glue at every configuration.

If every claim is held by some context, what each context allows concerns only the claims it holds, no context-free value fits what all the contexts allow, and some configuration keeps to what they allow, then no context-free frame fits them.
Parity is whether the number of holding claims among those a context counts is odd or even;
a parity system has a family of claims, and each context fixes the claims it counts and the parity it requires.
A contradiction is a family of contexts (repetition allowed) in which every claim is counted an even number of times while the required parities add up to odd.
For every context-free value, among the contexts of a contradiction it fits at most one fewer than their number, and so does any average over a mixture of values;
where each context has its own value, if each context can be fitted alone, all of them are fitted.

If the claims of the family are distinct and their sameness is decided, then for a listed family of contexts either there is a context-free value fitting each of them, or some family among them is a contradiction;
if every context is in the listed family, then there are values that keep to what the contexts allow and glue, exactly where there is no contradiction.
Meets is: the need is at most the level of the condition.
A formation at a step whose every dependence is met is said to have admission by the levels.
Bearing is a dependence whose need is positive.
For every formation that has admission at step A;

if at step B each of its conditions was already a condition of it at step A, its need is at most that at step A, and the level of the condition is not below that at step A, then it also has admission at step B.
Forms is: a dependence appears across a step: absent at the start of the step, present after it.
Dissolves is: a dependence disappears across a step: present at the start of the step, absent after it.
For every dependence absent at some step and present at some later step, that there is a step between at which it forms cannot be refuted;
if present at some step and absent at some later step, that there is a step between at which it dissolves cannot be refuted.
Kept is: a dependence is met at the start of a step, and after the step its level still meets the need at the start.
Broken is: a dependence is present and met at the start of a step, and after the step the level of its condition is below the need at the start.
Every dependence present and met at a step is, across this step, either kept or broken, and exactly one of the two.

If there is balance, a dependence meets, after a step, its need at the start of the step exactly where its need plus the joint taking is at most the level of its condition at the start plus what is given in all;

if the dependence is present and met at a step, then it is broken across this step exactly where the level of its condition at the start plus what is given in all falls short of its need plus the joint taking.
At the same condition and the same step, if one dependence is broken, then every dependence present and met whose need is not below that one is broken too.

If there is balance, only the active take, and they take only from what they draw on, then for every broken dependence there is an active relatum taking part that draws on its condition and takes from it at this step.

If there is balance, a dependence is broken, and for every relatum taking part at this step what it takes plus this need is at most the level at the start plus what is given in all, then what each relatum takes is less than the joint taking.

For another balanced flow, if at this step the level of this condition is not below that under the first flow, the joint taking is less than under the first flow by at least e, what is given in all is not less than under the first flow, and a need plus the joint taking of the first flow is at most the level under the first flow plus what it gives in all plus e, then this need is met after the step under the second flow.
Dependent is: at every step at which a formation is active it has admission: a supposition of a world, stated and not asserted.

Read taking and giving as a relation (a step may admit several kinds of taking and giving), and activity as taking part with some taking or giving: if dependence is read as necessarily no taking or giving (under every history that differs from the history read only in the level of this condition at this step, with that level below its need, no admissible taking and giving gives the formation any taking or giving), then every run of this relation is dependent, for any need;

if dependence is read as possibly no taking or giving (under these histories some admissible taking and giving gives the formation none), then there is a relation with a run of it that is not dependent.
If a law of taking and giving admits only one kind of taking and giving at each step, then on its runs both readings are the dependence that its law reads.

Under balance, where only the active give and the world is dependent: if the level of a condition is higher at the next step than at this step, then some relatum taking part and having admission gives to it at this step;

if a formation goes across a step from not having admission to having admission, and each of its dependences is still present across the step with need not decreasing, then it is not the case that none of its conditions has a relatum taking part with admission giving to it;

if no relatum of a region has admission at some step, from then on at every step each dependence of each relatum in the region is still present across the step with need not decreasing, and everything that gives to their conditions is in the region, then from then on no relatum of the region has admission.

If the world is dependent, the level of the condition of a dependence after a step is below the need at the start, and the dependence is still present after the step with need not decreased, then the formation is inactive after the step.

If the world is dependent and the level of a condition after some step is always below the need of a dependence at that step, then a formation still active afterwards cannot both still depend on this condition and have a need not below that at that step;
one whose dependence is still present after that step with need not below that at that step is never active from then on.

Broken does not decide what follows: there is a process with three runs from the same configuration that each break a dependence at step zero: in one run the level of the condition is below the need of step zero at every later step, and the formation is never active again;
in one run the same holds, but the dependence dissolves and another forms, and the formation is active at every step;
in one run the level of the condition is not below this need at every step, and from step two on the dependence is kept at every step.

title_en: Necessary condition and necessary and sufficient condition

clauses.en: A necessary condition is: with it, not necessarily so; without it, necessarily not so.
A necessary and sufficient condition is: with it, necessarily so; without it, necessarily not so.
If dependent, without admission there is no activity: admission is, for the activity of a formation, that without which it is necessarily not so;
that with it, it is not necessarily so (a case of admission without activity) has no named proof yet and is left open.
Ends is: a formation is never active from some step on.
If each formation of a family ends, then there is a step from which none of them is active.
A reserve is an amount of a formation that does not increase at a step at which the formation has no admission, and decreases if the formation is active at that step.
Dependent holds exactly where zero is a reserve.
For every reserve, if a formation from some step on never has admission, then its activity does not recur;
if its activity is decided at every step, then in any stretch from this step on the number of steps at which it is active is not more than its reserve at this step.

If there is balance, each relatum is paired with a condition, at steps at which the relatum has no admission nothing gives to this condition, and at steps at which it has no admission and is active something takes from it, then the level of this condition is a reserve of the relatum.
If a reserve falls whenever it is positive at a step without admission, then from the first step of never having admission, plus the reserve at that step, the formation is never active.
Embodied is: a relatum is active exactly where it stands as a condition.
If dependent, and at a step at which a formation is active it depends with positive need on an embodied relatum, then this embodied relatum is also active.
If the level of an embodied relatum after some step is always below the need of a dependence at that step, and this need is at most one, then the embodied relatum is not active afterwards.
When a web divided into two types is read as a web of one type of relata, no formation that is active at some step is embodied.
If dependent, at a step activity carries along a chain of dependence with positive need on embodied relata: if a relatum on the chain is active, then everything it reaches along the chain is active.
So if a relatum reached by the chain is not active at this step, then everything that reaches it along the chain is not active at this step; this is called coextinct.
Self-bearing is: at every step at which a relatum is active it depends with positive need on itself.
If dependent, a self-bearing relatum stands as a condition at every step at which it is active;
if it is also embodied, then its dependence on itself is met exactly where it is active.

If dependent, and an embodied, self-bearing relatum is active at a step and not active at the next, then everything that draws on it at this step draws on a condition at which some dependence is broken at that step.
There is a web in which two relata each depend only on the other and neither is self-bearing;
swapping the labels of their conditions, both are self-bearing and dependent holds as before: which relatum is self-bearing is fixed by the labelling.
Interacts is: two events are related through a condition: one draws on it and the other depends on it with positive need, whatever their steps.
Interaction runs both ways alike;
whatever interacts either depends on or draws on the condition through which it interacts.
If nothing draws on a condition, or nothing depends on it with positive need, then there is no interaction through it.
Whatever draws on a self-bearing relatum interacts with each of its active events.
Lives on is: a formation at a step draws on a relatum and depends on it with positive need.
If dependent, then for an active formation, what it lives on stands as a condition at this step;
if what it lives on is also embodied, it is also active at this step.
Arising is: a formation is not active at a step and is active at the next step;
ceasing is: a formation is active at a step and not active at the next step: arising and ceasing are activity coming to be and ceasing to be.

title_en: Comes to stand and ceases to stand

clauses.en: Comes to stand is: a condition has no level at a step and has a level at the next step;
ceases to stand is: a condition has a level at a step and has no level at the next step: coming to stand and ceasing to stand are standing as a condition coming to be and ceasing to be.
For every embodied relatum, if it arises, it comes to stand.
For every family of conditions, coming to stand recurs in the family exactly where ceasing to stand recurs in the family, without requiring that anything be decided.
Rises is: the level of a condition is higher at the next step than at this step;
falls is: it is lower at the next step than at this step.
For every amount counted in natural numbers, its value at the end of a stretch plus what it fell within the stretch equals its value at the start plus what it rose within the stretch;
the same holds of the sum of the amounts of a family.
For every family of conditions, if falling recurs in the family, then rising recurs in the family.
For every family whose members each have an amount counted in natural numbers, all bounded, if rising recurs in the family, then falling recurs in the family.
There is a web in which the level of a condition rises at every step and never falls.

Census balance is: within a stretch, the number of those for which a claim holds at the end plus the number of ceasings to be within the stretch equals the number of those for which it holds at the start plus the number of comings to be within the stretch.
Wherever the claims of the members of a family are decided, there is census balance.
Where those for which the claim holds are listed once each at every step and the claim is decided, there is also census balance, and the relata counted need not be finite;

read on activity: where the active are listed once each at every step and activity is decided, the number active at the end plus the number of ceasings within the stretch equals the number active at the start plus the number of arisings within the stretch.
Keeps pace is: within a stretch, the number of comings to be and the number of ceasings to be of the members of a family differ by at most the number of members.
Wherever the claims of the members of a family are decided, they keep pace, and coming to be recurs in the family exactly where ceasing to be recurs in the family;
where their claims are decided from some step on, this exactly-where also holds.
Without adding decided: if coming to be recurs in the family, then it cannot be said that from some step on nothing in the family ceases to be;
if ceasing to be recurs in the family, then it cannot be said that from some step on nothing in the family comes to be.
Wherever activity is decided and from some step on some family contains those active at each step (as holds where the formations are finite), arising recurs exactly where ceasing recurs.
Without adding decided, requiring of every finite world that 'arising recurs exactly where ceasing recurs' holds exactly where excluded middle holds;
if the activity of a finite world is decided from some step on, then arising recurs exactly where ceasing recurs.
A census is: the active at each step are listed once each.

For every claim decided at each step, if at arbitrarily late steps all those for which it holds lie in one family (as holds where those for which it holds have a census at each step): if ceasing to be recurs, then coming to be recurs;
read on activity: if ceasing recurs, then arising recurs.
The converse fails: there is a world with a census of the active in which arising recurs and ceasing does not recur;

for every bound that does not decrease along the steps and has no upper limit, there is a world with a census of the active at each step whose number does not exceed this bound, in which arising recurs and nothing ceases.
Where the active at each step have a census, activity is decided, and from some step on their number does not exceed a bound, arising recurs exactly where ceasing recurs.
A count is the tally of the members of a family for which a claim holds: the count exists exactly where the claim is decided for each member of the family.
Listing once is listing the members of a family, each once: a listing once exists exactly where the sameness of the members of the family is decided;
that a listing once exists cannot be refuted.

Wherever those for which a claim holds have a census at each step, their counts, without requiring decided, fit census balance at every step (the count at the earlier step is those listed at both steps plus those that cease to be; the count at the later step is those listed at both steps plus those that come to be);
a statement depending only on the values of the counts holds for every decided claim with a census exactly where it holds for every sequence of counts that fits census balance step by step.
With the sameness of relata read by their relations, the number of relata in every family of every world exists exactly where excluded middle holds.
Unceasing is: arising recurs.
If every arising, at a step at which nothing in a family rises, makes something in it fall: then, if unceasing holds, it cannot be said that from some step on nothing in the family rises;
if every rise is made by some active relatum giving to it, then it also cannot be said that from some step on the family has no active relatum giving to it.
For every amount counted in natural numbers, if it never rises and every arising makes it fall, then unceasing does not hold.
There is a web that fits all the if-clauses above, whose family has two conditions with a total level of one at every step, and which is unceasing;
there is a web in which every rise is made by some active relatum giving to it, rising recurs, active relata giving recur, and no relatum arises.
Coming to rest is: from some step on, in a world, no relatum arises and no relatum ceases.
Stillness is a configuration the law does not change.
For every law, its run from a starting configuration changes no more from some step on and satisfies a claim exactly where the run reaches a stillness that satisfies this claim.

Where the sameness of configurations is decided, all configurations of a run lie in one family, and the run has no configuration at some step that is had again later with a change in between: it changes no more from some step on exactly where at every step it is decided whether it changes again afterwards or changes no more;
that it changes no more from some step on cannot be refuted.

For every run of a law, where the sameness of configurations is decided and there is an amount counted in natural numbers that never falls along the run, rises whenever the configuration changes, and never exceeds the amount at the starting configuration plus d: the run changes no more from some step not beyond d, without requiring the limited principle of omniscience.
If a run changes no more from each of two steps on, then the configurations at the two steps are the same.

The limited principle of omniscience holds exactly where: for every process whose configurations have decided sameness and are exhausted by one family, if no configuration reachable from a configuration changes by a move to another configuration from which it can be reached again, then every run starting from this configuration changes no more from some step on.
The limited principle of omniscience also holds exactly where: for every run and every yes-or-no reading of its configurations, either the reading holds at some step or it holds at no step.

title_en: Continuation relation, continuation and arising anew

clauses.en: The continuation relation is the relation that reads a formation after a step as continuing a formation before the step.
Continuation is: a formation after a step is read by the continuation relation as continuing some formation active before the step.
Arises anew is: a formation is active after a step and continues no formation active before the step;
ceases without continuation is: a formation is active before a step and no active formation after the step continues it.
Taking as the continuation relation that each formation continues only itself, arising anew is arising and ceasing without continuation is ceasing.

title_en: Re-identification and co-reference within a step

clauses.en: Re-identification is a one-to-one correspondence at each step between two namings;
one whose correspondence is the same at every step is a renaming.
Co-reference within a step is two names picking out one relatum within a step: the correspondence a re-identification gives at each step.
Every re-identification of formations leaves unchanged, at each step, admission, kept and broken, and, at each step and each condition, what is taken and what is given.
Transformation is: the configuration differs across a step and continuation holds.
A world under a re-identification balances exactly where the continuations it reads all lie within balanced continuation, one to one at each step; this is a theorem without premise.
If a world balances, then f balance-continues g exactly where f and g have the same level after the step.

If a world balances and the sameness of relata is decided: every re-identification under which it still balances continues c as c exactly where after the step no other relatum has the same level as c;
if some other relatum d has the same level as c after a step, then there is a re-identification under which it still balances that continues c as d;
a relatum arises across a step under every re-identification under which the world still balances exactly where, by balanced continuation, it arises anew.

There is a world in which the levels of all relata are zero and both of two namings keep it balanced: under one naming it is unceasing, under the other nothing arises, and no arising is, by balanced continuation, an arising anew.
Continuity is: a re-identification keeps the name of a formation active both before and after a step.
Every re-identification with continuity makes no arising: an arising under the new names is also an arising under the old names;
so if unceasing holds under the new names, it also holds under the old names.
If the old names also keep continuity of the new names, then a formation active before a step and one active after it with the same name are one;
if there is continuity both ways, then arising and unceasing are exactly as they were.
There is a web and a re-identification with continuity that joins under one name two formations active in alternation: with separate names it is unceasing, with the joined name it is not unceasing;
the joined names keep the continuity of the separate names, and the separate names do not keep the continuity of the joined names.
Split is: one active formation before a step is continued by two active formations after the step;
merge is: one active formation after a step continues two active formations before the step.

Wherever the active at each step have a census and activity and the continuation relation are decided, at every step: if there is no split, then the number in the later census plus the number ceasing without continuation is at most the number in the earlier census plus the number arising anew;
if there is no merge, then it is not less;
if there is neither split nor merge, the two are equal.
So with a census and no split, if ceasing without continuation recurs, then arising anew recurs;
with a census and no merge, if from some step on the number listed does not exceed a bound and arising anew recurs, then ceasing without continuation recurs.

There is a web with a census of the active at each step: read by one continuation relation, it has no merge but has a split, at every step something ceases without continuation, and arising anew does not recur;
read by another continuation relation, it has no split but has a merge, at most two are listed at each step, at every step something arises anew, and nothing ceases without continuation.

For two families before and after a step, each with distinct members: under every continuation relation without split, not every member of the later family continues a member of the earlier family exactly where the later family has more members than the earlier.

Where the sameness of relata is decided: a continuation relation makes, for every two families of which the later has distinct members and more of them than the earlier, not every member of the later family continue a member of the earlier family, exactly where it has no split.

With a census of the active at each step: under every continuation relation without split, it recurs that the active after a step do not all continue those active before it exactly where it recurs that more are active after a step than before it.

If there is a census, the family taking part at each step has distinct members, only the active take and they take only from what they draw on, there are more without end, and the continuation relation is decided and has no split: then arising anew recurs.

There is a web that fits all of census, distinct members of the family taking part, only the active take and they take only from what they draw on, and more without end: read by one continuation relation with a split, arising anew still recurs;
read by another continuation relation with a split, nothing arises anew after the first step.
Persists is: a formation at a step is active, or depends on some condition at this step.
Hibernation is persisting without being active.
Reading activity as persisting: what persists before a step does not arise across this step;
an active formation ceases to persist across a step exactly where it ceases to be active and does not persist at the next step: entering hibernation is not ceasing.
If a re-identification keeps the names of what persists, then a relatum has only one name over every stretch in which it persists, active or in hibernation.
There is a web and a re-identification with continuity both ways that does not keep the names of what persists;
there is a web with a step at which nothing persists, in which a re-identification that keeps the names of what persists both ways still joins what comes before and after under one name.
A whole is active at each step exactly where one of the formations it joins is active;
the formations it joins are called its parts (for part see 一·一).
Every formation is the whole of itself;
there is a web with two formations, each active at every step, each of which is a whole of the other.
If a whole arises, then some part arises at the same step;
so if arising of a whole recurs, then arising recurs among its parts.
Under balance, if the uptake of a family is recurrently positive, then its replenishment cannot be zero at every step from some step on.
Under balance, if the takers of a family are more without end, then the replenishment of the family has no final bound;
if each relatum gives the family at most a fixed amount at each step, then the number of renewers also has no final bound.
Closed is: for a family at a step, no relatum taking part takes from outside the family or gives outside it.
A step has a closed family where some family with distinct members is closed at that step.
Enclosed around is: some family with distinct members contains this family and is closed at the step;
enclosed around what stands is: some family with distinct members contains everything that stands as a condition before or after the step and is closed at the step.
If all conditions lie in one family with distinct members, then every step has a closed family.
Where the sameness of conditions is decided, if a step has a closed family, then every family is enclosed around at that step;
without asking whether their sameness is decided, if a step has a closed family, that every family is enclosed around at it cannot be refuted.
Gainless is: for a family at a step, each relatum taking part gives the family no more than it takes from the family;
conserving is: it gives the family exactly what it takes from the family.

Under balance, if a family is gainless at a step, then the total level after the step plus the amount by which what is taken from the family at this step exceeds what is given to it equals the total level before the step;
if conserving, this amount is zero.

Under balance, if from some step on the family is conserving at every step and, once its configuration changes, it is never again the same as its configuration at any earlier step since that step, then the number of steps at which it changes is at most the number of ways its total level can be divided among its members;

if from some step on it is gainless at every step and its configuration changes recurringly, then 'after a change its configuration is again the same as at some earlier step since that step' cannot be refuted.
Dissipation is: for every family with distinct members closed at a step, each relatum taking part gives the family no more than it takes from it, and, if it takes something, less than it takes;
any family for which this holds at a step (without asking whether it is closed or whether its members are distinct) is said to dissipate at the step.
Under balance, if a family dissipates at a step, then the total level after the step plus the number of its takers is at most the total level before the step;

if over a stretch of steps the family balances and dissipates at every step, then the total level at the end of the stretch plus the total number of takers within it is at most the total level at the start of the stretch.
Under dissipation, if the step has a closed family, then every relatum taking part that gives also takes.
Depletion is: at every step at which a claim holds, if nothing in the family rises then something in it falls: this claim is said to deplete the family.
Under balance, if at every step at which a claim holds the family dissipates and has takers, then this claim depletes the family.
Under balance, if a family dissipates at a step and has takers, then something in the family falls, whether or not other members rise;
if a member of the family rises, then at the same step another member of the family falls.
Runs down is: at a step a family has distinct members, contains everything that stands as a condition before or after the step, and balances and dissipates.
For every family that runs down at a step, the level of some condition rises or falls exactly where the total level of the family falls.

Wherever what stands as a condition has a census, rising or falling of the level of a condition recurs exactly where there recur steps at which what stands does not run down and on which some level rises or falls.

Under balance and dissipation, where what stands has a census, if from some step on it cannot be refuted that what stands is enclosed around at every step, then taking and giving by relata taking part does not recur.
Wherever what stands has a census, if from some step on what stands runs down at every step, then no condition rises recurringly.

title_en: Conveying, fed from beyond, drawing in

clauses.en: Conveying is: a relatum taking part, at a step, takes from one condition and gives to a condition.
Fed from beyond is: at a step, a condition outside a family conveys into a member of the family.
A step without drawing in is one at which everything that gives to the family takes only from within the family;
drawing in is: not without drawing in.
Wherever the sameness of conditions is decided, a step is without drawing in exactly where there is no feeding from beyond at that step.

title_en: A family taken from recurringly is fed from beyond

clauses.en: Under balance and dissipation, if a family is taken from recurringly, then no family with distinct members that contains this family can be closed at every step from some step on.
If this family has distinct members and from some step on is enclosed around at every step, then it cannot be without drawing in at every step from some step on;
if the sameness of conditions is decided, then it also cannot be without feeding from beyond at every step from some step on.
If the sameness of conditions is decided and something in the family rises recurringly, it also cannot be without feeding from beyond at every step from some step on;
if relata are of one type with decided sameness and an embodied member of the family arises recurringly, the same holds.
A cut is a region that no relation leads out of.

Reading relation as conveying: if relata are of one type with decided sameness, there is balance and dissipation, a family has distinct members, from some step on it is enclosed around at every step, and it is taken from recurringly, then its region is not a cut.
Read as relata of one type, conveying relates two conditions, while neither interacts nor lives on relates two conditions.
Succession is: what is drawn on is, at every step, given to by sources that follow one another, and no source gives again.

There is a flow with balance and dissipation in which only the active give, one relatum takes from the pool at every step, the pool is fed from beyond at every step, and no source takes part at two steps or is active at two steps.
Openness is: it cannot be that from some step on every step has a closed family: taking and giving go beyond every family.
Every world in which the active have a census, all relata are embodied, and which balances, dissipates and is unceasing, has openness.

There is a world that is dependent and balances, in which only the active give, only the active take and they take only from what they draw on, which dissipates, is embodied and has a census of the active, and which has openness and is not unceasing.
Archimedean amounts is: for every amount greater than zero and any given amount, adding the first to itself some number of times goes beyond the given amount.
Least loss is the least amount, greater than zero, by which an amount falls at every step counted.
Amounts in natural numbers are Archimedean amounts.

title_en: Coming to rest needs a least loss

clauses.en: For every amount that does not rise from some step on and falls by at least a least loss at every step counted, if there is a number m such that m least losses added together go beyond its value at that step, then the steps counted do not recur.
If the amounts are Archimedean amounts, a least loss greater than zero suffices.

title_en: Read from a family, no least loss is needed

clauses.en: For every amount read from configurations contained in one family, if it does not rise from some step on, then strict falls do not recur;
this holds for any amounts, without a least loss and without Archimedean amounts.
Approaches without reaching is: an amount approaches coming to rest without reaching it.

For every Archimedean amount whose value at each step from some step on, plus what it falls, is at most its value before the step, for any ε greater than zero there is a number such that from this step on there are not that many steps each falling by at least ε;
steps falling by at least ε do not recur.
There are Archimedean amounts without a least loss, with a value among them that falls at every step and for which, for every ε greater than zero, steps falling by at least ε do not recur.

title_en: The law of coming to rest

clauses.en: For every world in which the active have a census, what stands has a census, everything that arises is embodied, and which balances, dissipates, and from some step on is enclosed around what stands at every step, 'it comes to rest from some step on' cannot be refuted.

If, for every finite world with decided activity that has the seven suppositions dependent, balance, only the active give, only the active take and they take only from what they draw on, dissipation, embodied, and a census of the active, the step from which nothing arises can be pointed out, then the limited principle of omniscience holds.

title_en: Coming to rest in any amounts

clauses.en: Reading the levels and the taking and giving of a world in any amounts: a family has no self-increase at a step where, for each member, its level after the step plus what is taken from it lies within its level before the step plus what is given to it (balance is the equality form of this: a balanced world read in natural-number amounts has no self-increase);
a family dissipates at a step where relata taking part give the family no more than they take, and those that give exactly what they take take nothing.
For every family with no self-increase that dissipates, if the level of a member of the family rises or falls, then the total level of the family strictly falls, without a least loss.

For every world in which the active have a census, all relata are embodied, there is no self-increase, it dissipates, from some step on every step has a closed family, and the total level of the active is read from configurations contained in one family, 'it comes to rest from some step on' cannot be refuted.

title_en: Joint excess and taking within giving

clauses.en: Joint excess is: the relata taking part jointly take from a condition at a step more than is given to it at that step;
taking within giving is: the joint taking is at most what is given;
each taking within giving is: each relatum taking part takes from a condition at a step no more than is given to it at this step.
Under balance, with taking within giving, the level does not fall at this step;
with taking within giving at every step, the level is not below its start.
Under balance, at every step of joint excess the level falls by at least one;
if from some step on there are n steps of joint excess, then the level after the n steps plus n is at most its start.
There is a condition at which, at a step, each taking is within giving and there is joint excess.

title_en: Joint excess ends what depends on the condition

clauses.en: Under balance, where only the active give, the world is dependent, and every renewer of a condition depends on it with need not below m: once the level is below m, it is below m at every step afterwards, and nothing that depends on it with need not below m is active.

If from some step on there are n steps of joint excess and the starting level is less than n + m, then after the n steps the level is below m at every step and nothing that depends on it with need not below m is active; takers that depend on it with such a need are among them.

The same holds for a family: if everything taking part that gives to a member of the family depends on some member of the family with need not below m, the family has joint excess at each of n steps from some step on, and the starting total level is less than n + m, then from then on nothing that depends on any member of the family with need not below m is active.

Under balance, if the family together with the conditions beyond it is gainless at a step, then the total level of both after the step plus the amount by which joint taking exceeds giving over the family and beyond equals the total level of both before the step;
if the family and what is beyond it dissipate at a step, then the total level of both after the step plus the number of takers over the family and beyond is at most the total level before the step.

If over a stretch of steps the family and what is beyond it are gainless at every step, then the total level of both at the end of the stretch is at most that at the start: the rise of the family is at most the fall beyond it.

If the total level of the family rises above the sum of the total levels of both at the start of the stretch, then it cannot be that the family and what is beyond it are gainless at every step of the stretch.

Under balance, if each condition beyond the family has a relatum depending on it with a need it meets, the family and what is beyond it are gainless at a step, and the total level of the family after the step plus the amount by which joint taking exceeds giving over the family and beyond is more than the total level of the family before the step plus the sum, over the conditions beyond, of the amount by which each level exceeds the need it meets, then some dependence beyond the family is broken.
Takes all is: a relatum taking part takes from a condition at a step no less than all that is given to it at that step.

For every condition given at most B at each step, if what a relatum takes is larger at the next step than at this step for n steps in a row, and n is greater than B, then at the end of the n steps this relatum, if taking part, takes all.
Under balance, no relatum can, for L + 1 steps from some step on, take part and take more than is given, where L is the starting level.

Under balance, where only the active give, the world is dependent, and every renewer of a condition depends on it with need not below m: if a relatum takes all for n steps while another relatum takes part and takes from the condition at each of these n steps, and the starting level is less than n + m, then from then on nothing that depends on the condition with need not below m is active, and so too for the one that takes all if it depends on it with such a need;

if a relatum takes all at every step, depends on the condition with need not below m at every step and is active at every step, then no other relatum can take part and take from it for L + 1 steps from any step, where L is the level at that step.
Runs dry is: a level falls to zero.

For every process in which at every step the level after the step plus what is taken at this step is at most the level before the step, and something is taken at every step at which the level is positive, every sequence of moves no shorter than its starting level ends at zero;
from a step at zero, nothing is taken.

title_en: The run-dry boundary under a standing draw

clauses.en: A condition at each step is first taken from by the standing draw H (all of it, if it is less than H), then given g(z) according to what is left z (the standing giving).
If g(z) is less than H whenever z is less than y, and g(0) is zero, then a level starting below H + y runs dry within as many steps as its starting level.

If g(z) is not less than H whenever z is not less than y and z + H is at most hi, and no step takes a level not above hi beyond hi, then a level starting from H + y up to hi never falls below its start and never exceeds hi.
If both hold and H + y is greater than zero, then a level starting not above hi eventually runs dry exactly where its start is less than H + y: H + y is called the run-dry boundary.
If g(z) is zero whenever z is less than the need m, H is positive, and y is the least z for which g(z) is not less than H, then m is less than y exactly where g(m) is less than H.

title_en: Where a run changes no more under a standing draw

clauses.en: If the standing giving does not decrease as what is left grows, and no step takes a level not above hi beyond hi, then a run starting from a level not above hi changes no more from some step not beyond hi, at a level that a step of the standing giving does not change.

There is a standing giving that gives two from zero and gives zero when what is left is more than zero, which does not increase with what is left, with standing draw one, in which no step takes a level not above two beyond two, and the run from one goes back and forth between one and two at every step and never reaches a step after which it changes no more.

If what is given is fixed by reading what is left and the preceding giving (write it A), A increases with both, and a step from a level and a preceding giving both not above hi has its next level not above hi: then for every preceding giving r not above hi, the run from a level x not above hi ends up changing no more from some step on below the standing draw exactly where x is below a threshold;
this threshold does not increase as r increases.

Where what is given reads only what is left (the standing giving g), g increases with what is left, the hypotheses of 四·二十四 hold, and the region not above hi reaches the run-dry boundary, the threshold is the run-dry boundary H + y for every r.
There is a giving that does not increase with what is left, keeps to its region, and has no threshold dividing its runs.
Return is: a configuration can still reach itself after a step: there is a move from it to a configuration from which it can be reached.
Under a law, a configuration returns exactly where the configuration of its run after some positive number of steps is this configuration.
For every process, a configuration that returns can be had at every step.
Confluence is: a law takes two different configurations in one step to one configuration.
For every two configurations in confluence, they share one configuration at every step afterwards, and they do not both return.
For every law, if a configuration cannot be had at some step, then it cannot be had at any step afterwards;
if the configurations are exhausted by one family and the law has confluence, then not every configuration can be had at step N (N being the number of members of the family).
Where the configurations are exhausted by one family, a law has no confluence exactly where every configuration returns, exactly where every configuration can be had at every step;
there, if an amount counted in natural numbers never falls along a run and rises at some step, then the law is not without confluence.
For every law without confluence that has a configuration that does not return, no family exhausts its configurations.

title_en: Confluence of the part is taken up by the rest

clauses.en: For every law without confluence, with each configuration read as its part and its rest, two configurations being one where both their parts and their rests are the same: if, after k pairwise distinct configurations each run n steps, their parts all lie in one family and their rests all lie in another, then the product of the numbers of members of the two families is not less than k;
so if the parts are all one, every family containing the rests has at least k members.
For every law without confluence, if after one step the part of every configuration is the same p, and some configuration has a part other than p, then no family exhausts the configurations.

For every process with a run whose configurations all lie in one family, and an amount whose value after each step plus what it loses at this step is at most its value before the step: if what it loses at some step is not within zero, then this process is not without confluence.
Novelty is: from some step on every configuration differs from every configuration before it.
For every family whose total level from some step on does not exceed a bound, from every step on there are two steps that share a configuration of this family.
For every history that has novelty from the start, or along which an amount counted in natural numbers rises at every step, no family exhausts what it passes through.
A prefix is the segment of a course before some step.
Kept history takes as configuration the pair of present and prefix: the present runs by the law, and the previous present enters the prefix.
For every law, with kept history it has no confluence, has novelty from the start, does not return, a configuration with an empty prefix cannot be had after one step, and no family exhausts its run;
if the present returns, the prefixes differ;
if the configurations a run of the law passes through are exhausted by one family, then from every step on there are two steps that share one present and differ in prefix.
An invariant is a region kept at every admissible step of a process: if a configuration is in the region, the outcome of an admissible step from it is in the region too.
A region is invariant exactly where every move keeps it.
For every invariant, everything reachable from the region is in the region.
For every run that is in a region at some step, if every move it takes afterwards keeps this region, then it is in the region at every step afterwards;
if a run leaves the region, the move at the step at which it leaves does not keep the region.
A gate is a decided label on the moves of a process.

If every move that is not a gate reflects a claim (if the claim holds at the configuration after the step, it holds at the configuration before the step too), then every sequence of moves ending at a configuration where this claim holds either starts at a configuration where it holds, or can be divided into an earlier segment, a step through a gate and a later segment, with the claim holding after this step through the gate;
this does not require that the claim be decided.
If every move that is not a gate leaves a quantity unchanged, then every sequence of moves that changes this quantity contains a move through a gate.

Where the gate is given by claims (whether each move is a gate is a claim) and every move that is not a gate reflects a claim: if whether each move is a gate is decided, then every sequence of moves ending at a configuration where the claim holds either starts at a configuration where it holds or contains a move through a gate;
requiring this for every process without supposing that the gate is decided holds exactly where every claim has double-negation stability.
An absorbing region is a region a law never leaves: if a configuration is in the region, its next configuration is in the region too.
The absorbing regions of a law are exactly the invariants of its process.
For every configuration, what it can reach from the next step on is an absorbing region;
the region of configurations that return is an absorbing region;
what can be had after n steps is an absorbing region.
If a run enters an absorbing region, it is in it at every step afterwards.
Drawn into is: a configuration is outside a region, and its run comes into the region.
A basin is the configurations drawn into an absorbing region from outside it.
For every law, a configuration is drawn into some absorbing region exactly where it does not return;
a configuration that does not return is drawn into the absorbing region of what it can reach from the next step on.
A configuration that cannot be had after n steps is drawn into the absorbing region of what can be had after n steps.
An attractor is an absorbing region all of whose configurations return and into which some configuration is drawn from outside.

If one family exhausts the configurations, then every run comes to configurations that return, and every configuration that does not return is drawn into the absorbing region of those that return: the region of returning configurations is an absorbing region, and those that do not return all lie in its basin.
If one family exhausts the configurations and their sameness is decided, then the law brings no two configurations to confluence exactly where no configuration is drawn into anything.

Where the configurations are infinite, there is a law under which a configuration is drawn into an absorbing region and there is no confluence: with successor as the law, zero is drawn into one, and no two configurations are in confluence.
Lock-in is: drawn into an absorbing region and not returning.
For every law, if a configuration is outside an absorbing region and its run enters it at some step, then from then on the run is never at this configuration again.
So (五·七) for every process, if a configuration is in an invariant, then from it no configuration outside the invariant can be reached;
along a run, if it is in an invariant from some step, then none of its later configurations is the configuration of any step at which it was outside the invariant.
Possibly drawn into is: a configuration is outside a region, and from it some configuration in the region can be reached;
necessarily drawn into is: a configuration is outside the region, and every run from it comes into the region.
For every process, a configuration is necessarily drawn into some invariant exactly where it does not return;
a configuration is possibly drawn into some invariant exactly where from it a configuration can be reached from which it cannot be reached.
Under a law, possibly drawn into and necessarily drawn into are both drawn into.
There is a process with a configuration that is possibly drawn into an invariant, is not necessarily drawn into it, and returns.
A juncture, for a configuration s, is a configuration after one step from which s can still be reached and after another step from which s cannot be reached.
The outcomes of the two steps of a juncture differ;
a juncture is possibly drawn into.

For every s that returns, if from s a configuration t can be reached and t cannot reach s, then it cannot be refuted that there is a juncture y: y can be reached from s, y goes in one step to a configuration z, and z can reach t and cannot reach s.
If, for every configuration reachable from s, whether it can reach s is decided, then this juncture can be pointed out;
the same holds if one family exhausts the configurations and whether a configuration can reach another in one step is decided.
If for every process every juncture at which something is lost could be pointed out, then the limited principle of omniscience would hold.
A configuration with many steps need not be a juncture: there is a process whose only configuration has one step for each natural number, and this configuration is not a juncture of it.
Keeping, for a configuration s, is the steps of a process after which s can still be reached;
the other steps of the process, after which s cannot be reached, are steps of lock-in (taking one, s cannot be reached again on this path;
if this step is on a path from s, then s is possibly drawn into, 五·十三).
A juncture is exactly a configuration at which both keeping and lock-in have steps.
Keeping keeps s: everything reachable from s through keeping can reach s through keeping.
For every sub-process that keeps s, the steps it takes on paths from s are all steps of keeping: keeping is the greatest that keeps s.
If s returns, then what keeping removes on paths from s is exactly the steps of lock-in at junctures.
Taking only steps of lock-in, s does not return.
If a process keeps s, then nothing reachable from s is a juncture for s.
Persistence through change is: a whole is active at every step from some step on, while each of its parts ends, or none of its parts is active at two steps some number of steps apart.
Let a whole be active at every step from some step on: if no part of it is active at two steps d steps apart, then afterwards no d consecutive steps can all be without some part arising;
if each of its parts ends and they have a census, then it cannot be that no part arises from some step on, and it also cannot be that no part outside any given family arises from some step on.
If each of its parts ends, they have a census, and from some step on no part arises, then the whole ends.

Passing on is: whatever carries a pattern at the next step either already carries it at this step or has it passed to it by something that carries it at this step: a pattern reaches a new carrier only by passing.
If there is passing on, then whatever begins to carry the pattern has it passed to it by something that carries it at the step before.
